concept.name: Put credit spread
concept.definition: A put credit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short put at a higher strike and a long put at a lower strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net credit. It is synonymous with the bull put spread: a moderately bullish-to-neutral position whose maximum gain is the credit and whose maximum loss is the strike width minus the credit.
concept.intuition: You sell a put betting the stock stays above your strike, and buy a cheaper lower-strike put as insurance so a sell-off cannot cost more than a known amount.
concept.mechanics: The net credit is kept in full if the underlying finishes at or above the short strike; the long put caps losses below the lower strike. By put-call parity its payoff closely mirrors the call debit spread at equivalent strikes.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K2 - K1) - net credit; breakeven = K2 - net credit, where K1 < K2 are the put strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Gap-down moves can blow through both strikes and realize maximum loss with no chance to adjust; short-leg assignment near expiration or before ex-dividend can leave unwanted long stock.
concept.misconceptions: Choosing far-OTM strikes for a high win rate does not create an edge: the credit shrinks toward fair compensation for the residual tail risk, and one maximum loss erases many wins.
concept.example: Sell the XYZ $100 put for $3.00, buy the $95 put for $1.00: net credit $2.00. If XYZ stays at or above $100, keep $200; at or below $95, lose $300.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
